To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the social turn in K–12 programming education is a shift in the focus of programming education that has gone from a predominantly tool-oriented, individualistic and computational thinking approach to one that is more sociologically and culturally situated and focused on computational participation.

the development of computational artifacts, tools, communities, and practices in K-12 education is shifting from an individual and tool-oriented focus towards one that is sociological and culturally grounded in digital media production and sharing.

the social turn in K–12 programming education can be characterized by three shifts: (1) from coding to creating applications, including the use of visual and block-based languages, (2) remixing and sharing, and (3), facilitating communities.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ways in which programming education is changing and the ways in which these changes are leading to the emergence of computational participation as a new paradigm in K-12 education.
how we might move from thinking to participation, and from computational thinking to participation in computational cultures.
how the social turn can help us to understand the role of programming in K-14 education and how it can inform future research in this area.

the social turn in K12 programming education is a move away from the traditional, tool-oriented, and individualistic approach to programming, towards an approach that is more sociologically and culturally informed and grounded in the creation, sharing, and remixing of digital artifacts.

the social turn in K12 programming is a move from computational thinking towards computational participation, which can lead us to a better understanding of how to engage students with programming in a way that is both relevant to them and meaningful to society.

the social turn in programming education is a move from computational thinking towards computational participation, and we argue that this is the next step in the evolution of K-12 computing education.

computational thinking is an important first step in learning to program, but it is not the only step.

the social turn in K12 programming education is a necessary next step to ensure that the computational thinking agenda does not remain a privileged discourse of the technologically and economically privileged, but rather a means to democratize computing and computing education.
the social turn in K12 programming is not only a natural extension to the computational thinking movement, but also a necessary one.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the social turn in K–12 programming education is not just an extension of the computational turn in education, but rather a new and important development in its own right.

the social turn in K12 programming education is an important and timely development, as it has the potential to broaden participation in computing, and to do so by engaging students in meaningful ways with computing and digital technologies.

the social turn is a necessary step towards broadening participation in programming, as it is through participation in the social and cultural dimensions of programming that learners develop a deeper understanding of the field, and in turn a deeper understanding of how computing is a part of the world around them.
